One hit could leave two stains. The client displayed a predicted effect, then received confirmation over the network and treated it as a new attack. Merging events too broadly caused the opposite problem: a real subsequent hit disappeared. The system began retaining the origin of evidence and matching confirmations. Entity numbers also needed care: an old wound could not be transferred to a new player who inherited a freed number.

A stain on a floor and a wound on a character need different coordinates. The first belongs to a level surface; the second must be attached to animated geometry. MD2 stores sequences of vertex frames, while MD5 uses a skeleton and weights. An approximate shell suitable for one format could slide or flicker on the other. Highlighting and control of model parts developed alongside this work: colouring a head, torso or another region had to match the actual pose, not an assumed shape. Testing covered moving players, their weapons, shadows and reflections.

blocks.caption: Highlighting and model parts. A separate colour setting depended on geometry, animation, model-format support and several rendering paths.

blocks.text: Player and item highlighting had existed since spring. Now it passed through more graphics layers: translucent colour could unexpectedly become solid; texture remained in one mode and disappeared in another. A screenshot could expose incorrect blending. Flicker was harder: sequences of frames had to be recorded and compared against model pose, depth and drawing order.

Blood on walls, water and AVFX puddles had different destination surfaces. Choosing the wrong floor left a stain in mid-air; an incorrect pool boundary spread it onto dry stone. Marks were checked on moving elements and in rooms temporarily out of view. Separate presets and settings slots let contact effects change while preserving the rest of a scene. The player's own blood was adjusted so it did not obscure the fight.
Stalls When the Camera Turned

By autumn, a high FPS figure no longer adequately described the client's speed. Brick geometry could render quickly for a long time, then unexpectedly rebuild as the camera turned. The cache discarded recently used data; looking back forced it to be built again. A diagnostic run counted 329 builds and 320 evictions, with individual delays approaching half a second. Making one operation faster would not solve the main problem: expensive preparation kept returning inside gameplay frames.

blocks.caption: Volumetric brickwork in Q2PRO-X 1.6: projecting bricks and recessed joints give the wall depth. Preparing this geometry became one of the tasks of the autumn optimisation work.

blocks.text: Stable data began to be prepared at map load or when a setting changed. Camera turns no longer continually rebuilt bricks, but the cache occupied about 1.7 GB on one demanding test map and 3.3 GB on another. Initial preparation had not disappeared either. The gain was in removing it from ordinary movement; smoother frames were paid for with memory and waiting before play.

Reflections exposed another source of unnecessary work. The world was rendered again for several planes, with complex skies calculated before walls that subsequently covered them. Drawing the sky moved behind opaque geometry, using the depth already available. In the heaviest measured case, the improvement was only from 43.6 to 44.6 frames per second. There was less wasted computation, but the reflected world remained expensive. Other effect combinations continued to be tested separately.

blocks.caption: Autumn scenery served both as a distinctive look and as a demanding measurement case. Weather was allowed to reach the same state before comparisons.

blocks.text: An autumn preset helped test the rejection of invisible work. Skipping what the camera cannot see is useful; stopping puddles from developing there is a bug. Rain must keep filling them without an observer. Separating world state from its presentation raised the average frame rate in one controlled, demanding scenario from 75.5 to 86 FPS, roughly fourteen per cent. Comparisons included the same wait in rain, tens of thousands of variants and frame checks. Runs that lost focus or activated the screensaver were excluded: they were not measuring the intended comparison.

The current Q2PRO-X 1.6 line continued work on particles, lighting, reflections, vegetation and seasonal materials. Performance HUD showed their cost, while render scale and post-processing helped tune the load. On 10 October, the version was still developing. Meanwhile, another kind of testing had appeared: instead of comparing frames, it required rewatching matches and asking why a new computer opponent had lost.
Effects, Individually

Q2PRO-X 1.6 divided ordinary particles into 68 Standard families. Blood, blaster trails, rocket smoke, sparks, teleports and railgun particles could be enabled, disabled and coloured independently. Ten ordinary AVFX families gained settings of their own: changing a standard weapon trail should not quietly recolour the atmosphere. Sky meteors, falling meteors and comets retained separate colour choices—they are different phenomena, even if each leaves a luminous trail.

Lighting and object visibility gained their own presets. Gameplay choices included bright, saturated, monochrome and ‘Nothing Extra’ looks, with separate lighting choices for AVFX. Such a preset did not enable rain or plants on the user's behalf; it set lighting conditions. Model highlighting, individual parts and ordinary bloom were saved in their own set. The atmosphere could change without losing the carefully chosen readability of an opponent.

Optional health-and-armour music ambience also appeared. Nine states tied the background music's mood to the player's protection, with crossfaded transitions. Single-player and deathmatch were enabled separately, and an explicitly selected online track or music preset took precedence. It offered another way to feel the character's condition, not another source of information about opponents.

Users could replace audio assets and intro music. Custom intro tracks required neither rebuilding the client nor using factory filenames: language-specific FLAC collections were supported, with duration taken from the file itself. If no suitable music existed, the visual intro remained. Packaging details belonged in the guide; what mattered to players was that their chosen appearance did not have to sound exactly as the release authors intended.

A small but useful addition retained the history of successful connections. Shared across mods, it let people return to the last server after restarting, or reconnect automatically if desired. Failed attempts and mere ping refreshes did not clutter it. Such a feature is easy to overlook beside complex graphics, though it shortens the journey from launching the client to playing every day.

blocks.caption: Q2PRO-X contact effects connect lighting and particles with events in combat.

chapters.title: OpenTDM-X: Teaching a Bot to Win
chapters.period: September 2026 · Early betas and OpenTDM-X Beta 10

blocks.text: A bot could hardly miss and still lose the map. It surrendered red armour, emerged from the lower floor under an opponent's railgun, then respawned unarmed in a room where someone was already waiting. After a few such encounters, the human had everything needed and could choose the fights. OpenTDM-X set out to create an opponent capable of breaking that pattern: recovering, taking away a favourable position and exploiting someone else's mistake.

Earlier bot projects were studied in September. Candidates included JABot from the ACE family and 3ZB2: one offered appealing separation between subsystems, the other detailed movement and combat cases. Other projects had limitations too. The Gladiator archive lacked the source for its intelligence library, while Eraser was missing some navigation code. Even complete source did not provide a ready-made, physically fair OpenTDM player. Some bots sent ordinary commands while also changing velocity directly. Importing an entire controller like that would quietly grant different movement capabilities.

OpenTDM supplied the rules: weapons, items, physics and scoring. Perception, goal selection and execution were written for the bot. Its skill parameter determined capabilities, including permitted knowledge of opponents. Even at high levels, that knowledge did not grant different physics. A real explosion propelled a rocket jump, and a fired rocket travelled the same path as a human player's rocket.
What a Match Recording Can Teach

q2duel5 was the first training map. A September analysis pass decoded 121 unique recording streams—more than a million rows of player state. The program found demos both in growing folders and inside archives, without reanalysing streams already read. Decisions then had to be reconstructed from those frames: which item a player sought, why they changed direction, what they did before shooting and where they went afterwards.

A successful escape is not always a useful lesson. A player may survive because of the chosen route—or because the opponent missed. Fragments were compared with other recordings and level geometry. Tricks were broken down into acceleration, take-off and landing: the action had to be reproduced, rather than simply arriving at the recorded coordinates.

In early tests, a bot approached the railgun and jumped away, leaving it behind. It dodged one grenade into the path of the next. It collected a chaingun but forgot the ammunition beside it. The log could dutifully report selecting a goal; the human saw an uncollected weapon and picked it up. The investigation had to find what interrupted an action one step from success and keep a nearby worthwhile goal active until completion.

By OpenTDM-X Beta 10, the bot knew compact q2duel5 well. It applied pressure, caught respawns and fired into exits. That build was kept for comparison: if new rules seemed to slow the bot down, it was run alongside the newer one and played again. Some complaints concerned older weaknesses. In public Beta 10 demos, a human could also strip its stack from above while it remained on the lower floor. Returning to the older build would not solve that.

With full control, a human began hunting spawn points. The bare bot again answered with a blaster from a poor position and died, although it could have moved towards weapons and armour while firing on the way. One proposal introduced an increasing pause after repeated quick deaths. In a match, it helped the opponent, who could collect the whole level before the next spawn. The rule was removed and a one-second respawn restored. The mistake became clear across a series of deaths; in isolation, the delay did indeed postpone one death.

blocks.caption: A route after spawning: reach cover and a weapon while retaining the ability to answer the opponent's fire.

chapters.title: Weapons and Four Personalities

blocks.text: A human advanced at point-blank range with a hyperblaster while the bot held a rocket launcher and stayed silent. It had not frozen: each rule was faithfully doing its job. One forbade wasting time switching weapons; another forbade firing at the risk of killing itself with the blast. Together, they produced the one outcome the player had insisted must never happen: several seconds under fire without a reply. The investigation worked backwards from a ready shot—what could the bot do now, and which decision deprived it of that opportunity?

Switching could be fatal too. A rocket almost finished a human off; the bot drew a super shotgun and died before the change completed. The time to the next shot from the raised weapon had to be compared with the time to the first shot from another. The railgun remained useful for an opening hit and catching a respawn. But in a close pursuit of a wounded opponent, a burst or a spread often hit more reliably. One list of ‘best weapons’ could not cover all these situations.
Chasing Around a Loop

On a looped map, a human ahead on score could stop fighting altogether. They listened for the bot and left by another corridor. The chase repeated, circuit after circuit. Interception needed route changes, exit control and quiet waiting; even the railgun mattered, because a held weapon can give itself away by sound. Once a weak opponent appeared in direct view, however, a detour lost its purpose. An elaborate manoeuvre could give the human time to rebuild their stack.

A similar choice followed a frag. An available shot at a respawn on compact q2duel5 was worth taking immediately; chasing across a larger level left armour and weapons unclaimed. Small items mattered too. A stimpack or shard could raise a stack beyond the threshold of a single railgun kill, giving an unarmed opponent another chance to escape. Item value was tied to travel distance and the next likely encounter.
Four Styles

Four styles appeared: default, arcade, defence and chaotic. The first retained the main tactics; the second favoured fast movement and fighting; the third favoured survival, stack and control. The fourth varied its preferences during a game. A style could be set in a bot's profile and changed temporarily by vote. Their introduction required another comparison of versions: default had grown weaker, while defence sometimes refused even an available frag.

Arcade initially exposed an overly literal reading of attack: a bare bot ran at a prepared human. Active combat still requires a weapon, ammunition and protection; useful items along the way had to retain their place in the route. Defence made the opposite mistake, releasing an almost-finished opponent and ignoring a safe pickup. Changes to both styles returned to q2duel5, where speed and pressure already had a standard for comparison.

The shooting scale below skill 100 was checked separately. Low levels sometimes retained such accurate railgun aim that difficulty differences lost meaning. Accuracy reduction was made gradual without altering shooting at 100 or above. Adaptive ping had to be traced from behaviour to the server's response to an external browser. The mod's scoreboard could show latency for a bot while the browser still showed zero. Correcting that number was checked separately from perception and action timing.

OpenTDM-X Beta 11 was accepted for public installation on 4 October. Styles, weapon behaviour, pressure, escapes from poor positions and new profiles formed one package. Its change list compared it with the server's Beta 10. Long chains of internal fixes were reduced to their outcome: a server operator needed to install an update, not reconstruct its history from intermediate archives.

blocks.caption: Play styles change decision priorities while sharing the same shooting and movement rules.

chapters.title: Red Armour, Megahealth and Teleports

blocks.text: On ztn2dm3, the bot that played q2duel5 confidently often looked like a beginner. Here there was red armour, megahealth and open space. A rocket had travelled only part of the distance while the human had already fired a rail and stepped aside. The bot collected a weapon but left the megahealth, missed an item jump and walked away, or lost seconds on the stairs by adrenaline. On this map, its former accuracy could not compensate for the stack it surrendered.

One human route took only seconds: rocket launcher and ammunition, yellow armour, then a rocket jump to the chaingun. Next came its ammunition, two health packs along the way and red armour. Health partly repaid the jump's cost, and two strong weapons were now available. The bot was taught to complete this sequence quickly and adjust it if an item had already been taken. Early versions instead wavered between goals; during that hesitation, the human reached the red armour.

At the step before the railgun, the bot learned the trick and still sometimes left the weapon behind. It landed on the platform, noticed another goal and jumped away; elsewhere, it repeated the jump despite the railgun having just been collected. The whole sequence needed checking: starting position, acceleration, item contact and the next step. A graceful landing alone no longer counted as success.
Lifts and Fire into Cover

Lifts exposed several independent weaknesses. Waiting-for-platform state prevented the bot from finding a firing position even while an opponent rose directly in front of it. A rocket could fly towards where the human stood when fire was pressed and strike the floor after they had ascended. Platform speed and direction, flight time and possible movement changes had to be considered. If a player's protruding body hit an obstacle and the lift stopped or reversed, the old prediction was no longer valid. Falling under a platform required separate navigation recovery; better aiming could not solve it.

Rockets and grenades also had to be checked against room geometry. A human in the megahealth niche could hide their model while remaining within blast range of a wall. A grenade launcher could bounce a projectile around a corner; aiming directly at the body discarded that advantage. Yet endlessly firing into an empty exit consumed every round. Recordings showed both faults: silence beside an occupied niche and shooting the last rocket at somewhere the opponent had long since left.

Individual profiles developed in OpenTDM-X Beta 11.1 as well. Chat lines came from available references, greetings accounted for the current person and connection history, and replies to smileys ceased to be a constant echo. One mixed profile gained special behaviour when far ahead: do not immediately attack an unarmed respawn, approach, drop a weapon with ammunition and allow a few seconds to settle in. This rule applied only to that profile. A projectile already in flight did not become harmless—friendliness did not rewrite physics. Other bots continued the ordinary contest for the result.

An Ubuntu 22.04 build was prepared for public OpenTDM-X Beta 11.1. Package checks found an outdated example server configuration and unrelated client files in the source archive. The packages were rebuilt, separating the mod from the rest of the working folder. Installation and documentation were checked on both platforms.

OpenTDM-X Beta 11.2 with q3t2 was accepted and released on 8 October. Teleports moved players instantly and jump pads sharply changed velocity; those transitions could no longer be judged as ordinary running or a broken route. Afterwards, the bot continued towards its next goal. Previous maps remained in testing. On ztn2dm3, moving rocket jumps still needed speeding up, long-range combat choices needed work and delays around adrenaline remained. The next, still unfinished OpenTDM-X Beta 11.3 was addressing them.

blocks.caption: A teleport and a jump pad interrupt an ordinary route in different ways. This diagram explains the transitions, not q3t2's geometry.

chapters.title: From Studying Demos to Building Tools

blocks.text: Analysing everything by hand was becoming harder. Mapgen Studio emerged as a separate application for maps: base layouts, donors, transitions, a library and checks. Bot Training Studio took on demos and geometry, analysis and training. Users would add recordings and obtain knowledge files. They would not need to rebuild the game library for every new map.

blocks.caption: Mapgen Studio is a separate application for working with maps. Its development alongside the client helped shape the requirements for the next studio.

blocks.text: The model in Bot Training Studio works before a match. It can spend time analysing material on a GPU; the finished server bot must respond without that pause. Training was separated from execution. Model sizes were matched to available memory, with NVIDIA, AMD, Intel and a CPU fallback investigated. Readiness differed between options: seeing a device in a menu did not mean training, performance and results had been verified on it.

The studio's first launches brought down-to-earth problems. While Python was being checked, controls appeared and disappeared in the main window, and a single graphics card appeared several times in the list. Environment checking moved into the startup process. Libraries were included in the package, with installation of a compatible Python available when needed. Russian and English interfaces, hints, version history and updating followed.

Long-running tasks moved into the background: the window remained usable, jobs could be cancelled and exiting produced a warning. Indicators showed CPU, GPU and memory load. The factory model was separated from user additions; otherwise, an application update would overwrite hours of somebody else's training. Export began to account for data provenance and compatibility, while interrupted jobs retained their saved state.
A Teleport on a Graph

After q3t2 was accepted, its matches and separate trick recordings joined the training programme. A large coordinate jump on a graph might be a teleport, respawn, jump pad or recording gap. Mixing them would teach the model the wrong movement lesson. Events were therefore matched against trigger geometry, exit directions and subsequent states. The verified material included 64 full match recordings and 29 movement recordings. They showed not just where a person moved, but which mechanic made that movement possible.

Models were trained on NVIDIA and checked against held-out recordings. Some movement and transition measures improved. Related demos stayed on the same side of the dataset split: neighbouring frames from one match are too similar to count as an independent examination. Weapon choice, resource control and trick execution remained unresolved. On 10 October, the studio could already run training, but its results could not yet automatically produce a complete, strong duellist.

A baseline for unfamiliar maps was planned next. A bot would study routes and items during warmup, save a foundation shared by all profiles, then enrich it through matches. The studio would accept those files or start from geometry itself, with or without demos. A separate competition design proposed fixed conditions and comparisons between versions. At the book's cutoff, both remained plans.

blocks.caption: The plan for further learning combines geometry, demos and match experience. This diagram describes an intention, not a finished feature.

chapters.title: The First Launch

blocks.text: After installing Q2PRO-X, you can begin with the same configuration and server you used before. New settings do not demand an immediate change to the way you play. Then, on a free evening, open a familiar map without an opponent and walk through it more slowly: watch rain drain from an upper platform, see the Moon reflected, or examine a passage under different light. Or open one of your demos and finally discover how an opponent managed to arrive first.

A match usually calls for readable models, distinct sound and a steady response. During a walk, there is room for a different sky, weather and wildlife. Bots offer more things to try: repeat a trick, practise defence or arrange an open duel. Work on them continues, including through recordings in which a human has found yet another way to outwit them.

Builds and guides are available at q2pro-x.com. A good place to begin is a level you know by heart: walk to a weapon, take a lift, check movement and fire a shot. Changes are easier to notice there. Then you can join a server. Once somebody is collecting armour behind the wall, there is no time left to browse the menus.

blocks.caption: A familiar Q2PRO-X map in autumn scenery: the geometry remains recognisable while its surfaces look different.

chapters.title: Counting the Work Behind the Project

In that time, the client grew from early checks of controls and weapon prediction into a broad collection of graphics, networking and user features, alongside a bot mod and independent studios. The main dates below provide bearings in that crowded history. Client version numbers and OpenTDM-X beta numbers belong to different development lines and should not be read as a single sequence.

blocks.text: What the Archive Can Tell Us

The examined archive contained 776 documents setting out tasks. Of these, 520 were main or follow-up assignments, and 256 held accompanying requirements and corrections. Exact content duplicates were excluded; reports of results were not counted as new assignments. This is a document count, not a count of independent features. One capability could generate a long chain of clarifications, especially when a fix returned from an unsuccessful test. The examined documentary collection contained 3,245 Markdown files in total, of which 3,110 had distinct contents.

A snapshot of four related Git trees yielded 9,294 unique commits, 4,739 of which touched code within the chosen scope. Initial source imports, third-party files and automatically generated files were excluded. Available branches included experiments and intermediate builds. A commit here therefore means a recorded change, not a separately finished feature. One idea might pass through several rewrites; a change transferred under another hash also remains a separate record.

The chart begins in June because the available code history does not cover March–May in a comparable form. An early tree import cannot be presented as the entire project having been written at once. October ends at the book's cutoff. The same snapshot counted 984,895 added lines, 102,743 deletions and 2,735 code-file paths. These describe editing events: a line could be rewritten repeatedly or removed after an experiment. They are neither the final program's size nor a measure from which development productivity can be calculated.
Time Spent Testing Again

The archive preserves many checks in detail, but it is not a continuous timesheet. It cannot honestly yield the total hours of development, repeated matches, demo analysis and waiting for builds. A report date does not say how many uninterrupted hours the work took; a demo's duration is not the time spent studying it. Instead of an invented enormous total, this book offers concrete evidence: successive early betas, repeated failures after material fixes, eight rounds of network tests, demanding-scene comparisons and dozens of public recordings used to investigate tactics.

Some work inevitably had to be repeated: revisit an episode already fixed, retake measurements with matching configurations, launch an older build for comparison or play another match after changing one rule. Five returns to material re-enabling left users with one working setting. Faster shader preparation added no menu item, but shortened the wait. The change history reflects that work; counting only new features scarcely notices it.

blocks.caption: The next section groups capabilities by their use, from controls to preparing maps and bots.

blocks.text: The project's capabilities could be grouped into 99 subject areas. Successive fixes to one function were not counted as new features, and large effect families were not divided into every slider. The list includes everyday player tools as well as independent applications for preparing maps and training bots.

chapters.title: What You Can Do in the Game
chapters.period: The client, the mod and independent applications

blocks.text: There is no need to enable everything on a first visit. Begin with familiar controls and a server search, then watch one of your match recordings or change the weather on a map you know. The following pages gather the capabilities discussed in the book according to what they let a player do.
Adjust Movement and Shooting

A player presses fire and wants to see the shot immediately. Q2PRO-X can display it before the server's reply arrives: this is weapon prediction. The server still decides whether the projectile hit and how much damage it caused. Another system, Laghax, softens jolts when the server corrects a player's position. Its indicator shows latency, its variation and prediction state.

Mouse handling and a supported movement mode can be selected, a familiar fullscreen view retained or windowed play used. Players accustomed to 4:3 need not stretch the picture over a wide monitor: bars remain at the sides. Render scale and subsequent processing offer a choice between sharpness and GPU load.
Find a Server and Talk to Your Team

The server list supports searching for a game, filtering unsuitable choices and saving favourite addresses. In a match, voice chat removes the need to type while running. Microphones are selected in the game, and speech can be transmitted by holding a button or by voice activation. OpenTDM team matches gain additional teammate information on screen. Connection history makes it possible to return to a visited server after restarting the client.

When movement suddenly becomes uneven, it helps to distinguish a slow computer from an unstable connection. Network God settings, ping-adapted prediction and Network Lab tools allow those cases to be examined. Average latency is not the only important measure: how much it changes between packets matters too.
Understand Settings and Keep Your Habits

There is no need to remember hundreds of console commands. Menus with explanations lead to the required setting; a separate game-variable search reaches the details. The interface can switch between Russian and English. Fonts, startup presentation and personal frag messages also form part of client customisation. Console messages are categorised to make useful lines easier to find among service output.

An old configuration should not obstruct an update. The client therefore retained compatible ways of handling settings and separated preferences for ordinary play, mods and demo viewing. OLED screens have protection during inactivity.

Players and items can be highlighted, including individual model parts. Timers help track item returns where the game mode permits them. When an attractive scene becomes too demanding, the performance display helps identify where frame time is being spent.
Change a Familiar Map's Weather and Appearance

Rain and snow can fall on a familiar level. Water collects and reflects the surroundings, snow changes the surface and drops appear on a wet lens. Lava, foam and bubbles have their own effects. Materials, vegetation, ivy and autumn looks transform the same walls, courtyards and stairs in different ways.

Above the map, there can be weather skies, stars from an astronomical catalogue, the Moon and other celestial bodies. Meteors, comets, eclipses, black holes and sunbeams are available. High-dynamic-range, lighting and visibility settings determine how they look beside a dark passage or bright explosion.

Impacts, blood and other traces of combat connect the image with events in a match. Particle groups are adjusted separately. Every combination need not be assembled by hand: supplied presets and the generator let people choose an overall look and then refine it. Surfaces can gain hardware relief, mirrors and personal drawings; the air can gain volumetric clouds, fog and placed steam. Hardware tessellation depends on the selected graphics backend.
Revisit a Match or Play Without a Server

A recording can be found in the library, opened in the expanded player and navigated to an interesting moment. Multiview recordings support jumping to the next frag. Personal statistics offer another view of past games, while playback visuals let a scene be examined differently from the way it appeared during combat.

Sound adapts to the way people play: spatial processing for headphones, room reverberation and separate category volumes are available. Online music exists alongside game sounds without requiring their master volume to change. Music presets pair a scene with a track, while optional ambience changes with the character's health and armour.

A dedicated game DLL can alter single-player: shuffle items and monsters, turn water into real lava and reverse the change. Monster appearance and visible geometry can vary separately. Multiplayer maps support local monster training with item respawns and scoring; Free World offers more room for walking and observation. A bridge to 32-bit game modules helps run older additions.
Choose a Computer Opponent

OpenTDM-X is a separate mod with duel bots. Opponents have a skill level and style: balanced, offensive, defensive or changeable. A style can be attached to a profile and changed temporarily before a match. Bots learn to gather weapons and armour, finish a favourable fight, escape exposed positions and use suppressive fire, tricks and rocket jumps.

On q2duel5, narrow passages and pressure after respawning are especially important. ztn2dm3 adds red armour, megahealth and dangerous open areas. q3t2 requires teleports and jump pads to be understood. Yet choosing weapons, collecting ammunition and seeking cover must work on any map.

Lower difficulties receive less accurate shooting; ping adaptation accounts for delay when playing a human. Profiles have their own chat lines: greetings, occasional smiley replies, introductions and help. One mixed personality can ease pressure when far ahead and share a weapon with an unarmed opponent. Mod packages are available for Windows and Ubuntu 22.04.
Prepare a Map and Training Material

Mapgen Studio runs separately from the game. Users select a base map, add parts of other levels, connect transitions and check the result. Its library helps store prepared variants and return to them.

blocks.caption: Keeping factory data and personal additions separate protects the user's work when the studio is updated.

blocks.text: Bot Training Studio has a different purpose: loading match and trick recordings, analysing movement and preparing material for local training. Factory data and user additions are kept separate so an update does not erase personal work. Long jobs run in the background; the interface remains available and shows resource use. GPU and CPU options, version history, updating and a prepared runtime environment are provided.

By the date of this book, demo analysis and initial training experiments were working. Producing complete tactical behaviour for a new map still required research and in-game checks. The studio is not presented as a finished, one-click way to create an unbeatable opponent.
